what_its_for: Oritavancin is an antibiotic used to treat certain serious bacterial skin infections in adults, including infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus (staph), including the hard-to-treat MRSA strain. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein, usually in a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. You will not be giving this medication to yourself at home. The IV infusion is given slowly over 3 hours. You will typically receive only ONE dose total for your entire treatment course, though your doctor will decide what is right for you.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 1,200 mg given as a single IV infusion over 3 hours. This single dose is often all the treatment you need. Your doctor may adjust the dose or schedule based on your specific situation. Do not try to change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medication is given by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting, it is very unlikely you will miss a dose. If you miss or need to reschedule your infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away so they can arrange a new time for you as soon as possible.
storage: You will not need to store this medication at home since it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. If you are told anything about storing prepared doses, keep them refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and use within the time your pharmacist specifies. Never freeze the prepared solution.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you take blood thinners like warfarin (Coumadin) because oritavancin can affect how these drugs work in your body for several days after your infusion. Avoid starting new medications without telling your doctor first. Do not use unfractionated (regular) heparin for at least 48 hours after receiving this drug, as it may cause inaccurate lab test results. Limit alcohol use while recovering from your infection.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency care right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (hives, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing); redness, flushing, or itching of your face, neck, or upper body during or after the infusion (a reaction sometimes called 'Red Man Syndrome'); chest pain or fast heartbeat; signs of a new infection such as worsening redness, warmth, swelling, or drainage at the wound site; severe diarrhea or stomach cramps (which could signal a serious gut infection); dizziness or fainting; or any other unusual or concerning symptoms after your treatment.
when_it_works: Many patients start to feel better within 2 to 3 days after receiving their infusion. Because oritavancin stays active in your body for a long time, a single dose can treat your infection over the course of several days. If you do not feel better within a few days or if your symptoms get worse, contact your doctor right away.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): No dose adjustment is needed, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: No routine dose adjustment is required, but let your doctor know about any kidney or liver issues. Pregnant women: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. The safety of this drug during pregnancy is not fully established, so your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks with you. Breastfeeding mothers: It is not known if this drug passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the safest option for you and your baby. Children: This medication is currently approved only for adults. Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
